title: VPN and IPsec Concepts
summary: Covers VPN types (remote-access vs. site-to-site), VPN technologies such as GRE, GRE over IPsec, and DMVPN, and the IPsec security framework including AH/ESP, IKE phases, transport vs. tunnel mode, and the algorithms providing confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and key exchange.

commands.description: Creates and enters configuration for a logical GRE tunnel interface, used to encapsulate a wide variety of traffic (including multicast/broadcast, e.g., routing-protocol traffic) between two endpoints.
Specifies the local source interface or IP address for a GRE tunnel.
Specifies the remote endpoint IP address for a GRE tunnel.
Explicitly sets a tunnel interface's encapsulation to GRE over IP, the default mode for Cisco tunnel interfaces.

Creates an IKE Phase 1 (ISAKMP) policy defining the parameters (encryption algorithm, hash, authentication method, DH group, lifetime) used to negotiate the secure management tunnel between IPsec peers.
Defines the combination of IPsec security protocols and algorithms (e.g., ESP encryption and authentication) used to protect data during IKE Phase 2 (the IPsec data tunnel).
Configures the pre-shared key (PSK) used to authenticate the IKE Phase 1 peer at the specified address.
Creates a crypto map entry that ties together the peer, transform-set, and interesting-traffic ACL for a site-to-site IPsec VPN.
Within a crypto map entry, specifies the remote IPsec peer's IP address.
Within a crypto map entry, specifies which IPsec transform-set defines the encryption/authentication algorithms for the tunnel.
Within a crypto map entry, references the ACL that defines the 'interesting traffic' to be encrypted by the IPsec tunnel.
Applied under an interface to activate the referenced crypto map, enabling IPsec encryption on traffic leaving that interface.

terms.description: A technology that uses virtual (logical) connections routed through a public network (such as the internet) to create a private network path, rather than using dedicated physical connections.
A VPN type where an individual user's device runs client software (or a browser) to dynamically connect to a private network over the internet — e.g., a telecommuter connecting from a hotel.
An 'always on' VPN connection between two VPN gateways that joins two entire networks together; users at each site need no special client software or configuration.

An open-standards framework, relying on existing algorithms, that provides confidentiality (encryption via AES/DES/3DES), data integrity (hashing via MD5/SHA), origin authentication (via IKE), and secure key exchange (via Diffie-Hellman) for both site-to-site and remote-access VPNs.

The IPsec protocol used to authenticate IPsec peers (via PSK, digital certificates, etc.) and to negotiate/establish the security associations and keys used for the tunnel; operates in two phases (Phase 1 establishes a secure ISAKMP management tunnel, Phase 2 negotiates the actual IPsec SAs).
A key-exchange algorithm that lets two peers establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel; used by IPsec for secure key exchange, not for encryption or hashing itself.
Hashing algorithms used by IPsec (via HMAC) to provide data integrity — verifying data was not altered in transit — as opposed to AES/DES which provide confidentiality via encryption.

A Cisco tunneling protocol that encapsulates a wide variety of protocol packet types, including multicast and broadcast traffic (needed for dynamic routing protocols). GRE itself provides no encryption, so it is often paired with IPsec (GRE over IPsec).

A GRE variant letting one tunnel interface support multiple dynamically created tunnel endpoints; provides the hub in DMVPN a permanent tunnel source while spoke tunnel destinations are created dynamically.

A Cisco solution for building a scalable, dynamic mesh of secure spoke tunnels from a central hub, built on three component protocols: NHRP (address mapping), IPsec (encryption), and mGRE (dynamic multipoint tunneling).
The distributed address-mapping protocol used in DMVPN so that spoke routers can dynamically resolve the public IP address of the hub (and other spokes) needed to establish tunnels.
Cisco's remote-access VPN client. If not preinstalled, the user first makes a clientless SSL VPN connection via a web browser, which then offers the AnyConnect client for download and installation.
A remote-access VPN accessed entirely through a standard, compliant web browser without any preinstalled VPN client software.

terms.full: Secure Sockets Layer VPN / Transport Layer Security
terms.description: A remote-access VPN type negotiated using TLS (the modern successor to SSL); preferred for remote access because it typically requires only a web browser, giving lower deployment complexity than IPsec client VPNs.

A service-provider-managed VPN where traffic is forwarded across the provider's MPLS backbone using labels pre-distributed among core routers, creating segregated, secure virtual paths between customer sites.

GRE has no built-in encryption; encapsulating GRE inside IPsec adds encryption/authentication while still allowing multicast and routing-protocol traffic to traverse the tunnel, which plain IPsec cannot carry alone.

Applies IPsec configuration to a logical, routable virtual interface rather than a physical interface; packets routed to the VTI are automatically encrypted and forwarded, and it natively supports unicast and multicast traffic without separate GRE encapsulation.

The four pillars of secure communications: confidentiality (encryption), integrity (hashing), origin authentication (message truly from claimed sender), and non-repudiation (sender cannot deny having sent it).

terms.full: Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol
terms.description: The framework used by IKE Phase 1 to establish a secure, authenticated management channel between IPsec peers before the actual IPsec (Phase 2) security associations are negotiated.
An IPsec security protocol that provides data integrity and origin authentication but no confidentiality (no encryption); largely superseded by ESP in practice.
An IPsec security protocol that provides confidentiality (encryption) in addition to data integrity and authentication, making it the more commonly used IPsec protocol compared to AH.

terms.full: IPsec Transport Mode vs Tunnel Mode
terms.description: Transport mode encrypts/authenticates only the original packet's payload, keeping the original IP header intact (used end-to-end between hosts); tunnel mode encapsulates the entire original packet inside a new IP header (used between gateways in site-to-site VPNs).

terms.full: IPsec VPN, GRE over IPsec, Cisco DMVPN
terms.description: VPN types created and managed by the enterprise itself using its own infrastructure to connect sites/branch offices, as opposed to service-provider-managed (e.g., MPLS L3 VPN) or remote-access VPN types.
A shared secret manually configured on both IPsec peers and used by IKE Phase 1 to mutually authenticate the peers before building the secure ISAKMP session.
The negotiated agreement between two IPsec peers (algorithms, keys, lifetimes) that governs how a particular traffic flow is protected; separate SAs exist for ISAKMP (Phase 1) and IPsec (Phase 2).
An IPsec option that generates a fresh Diffie-Hellman key exchange for each new SA, so compromise of one key does not expose data protected by past or future keys.

facts: A VPN uses virtual (logical) connections routed through a public network like the internet to create a private network path, instead of using dedicated physical circuits.

Remote-access VPNs let an individual host dynamically connect via client software or a browser; site-to-site VPNs are 'always on' connections between two VPN gateways joining entire networks, requiring no client software on end hosts.

IPsec is an open-standards (non-proprietary) framework providing confidentiality (AES/DES/3DES encryption), integrity (MD5/SHA hashing), origin authentication and key negotiation (IKE), and secure key exchange (Diffie-Hellman).

IPsec's two core protocols are AH (Authentication Header, IP protocol 51 — provides integrity and authentication but no encryption) and ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload, IP protocol 50 — provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication).

IKE negotiates the IPsec tunnel in two phases: Phase 1 establishes a secure, bidirectional ISAKMP session between peers (main or aggressive mode); Phase 2 negotiates the actual IPsec security associations used to protect data traffic (quick mode).

IPsec tunnel mode encrypts and encapsulates the entire original IP packet with a new IP header (used for site-to-site VPNs); transport mode encrypts only the payload, leaving the original IP header intact (used for host-to-host traffic).

GRE tunnels can encapsulate multicast/broadcast traffic (needed for dynamic routing protocols) but provide no encryption on their own; GRE over IPsec combines GRE's protocol flexibility with IPsec's encryption since plain IPsec carries unicast traffic only.

DMVPN combines NHRP (dynamic address mapping), IPsec (encryption), and mGRE (a single interface supporting multiple dynamically created spoke tunnels) to build a scalable hub-and-spoke or dynamic full-mesh VPN.
An IPsec Virtual Tunnel Interface (VTI) applies IPsec to a logical routable interface and natively supports both unicast and multicast traffic without needing separate GRE encapsulation.

Clientless SSL/TLS VPNs need only a standard web browser for remote access, offering lower deployment complexity than IPsec client VPNs; Cisco AnyConnect can be pushed to the client after an initial clientless SSL connection.
IKE Phase 1 peers authenticate each other using either pre-shared keys (PSK) or RSA digital signatures/certificates before the secure ISAKMP tunnel used to negotiate Phase 2 IPsec SAs is established.

A Security Association (SA) is the negotiated set of parameters (encryption/hash algorithms, keys, lifetime) governing protection of a traffic flow; separate SAs exist for the IKE/ISAKMP Phase 1 session and for each Phase 2 IPsec (AH/ESP) flow, and they are typically unidirectional so two SAs exist per direction of a session.

A site-to-site IPsec VPN is configured with a crypto map that ties together the peer address (set peer), the encryption/authentication algorithms (set transform-set), and the 'interesting traffic' ACL (match address); the crypto map is then applied to the outbound-facing interface.

questions.questionHtml: Which two IPsec protocols are used to provide data integrity?
questions.explanationHtml: The IPsec framework uses various protocols and algorithms to provide data confidentiality, data integrity, authentication, and secure key exchange. Two popular algorithms used to ensure that data is not intercepted and modified (data integrity) are MD5 and SHA. AES is an encryption protocol and provides data confidentiality. DH (Diffie-Hellman) is an algorithm used for key exchange. RSA is an algorithm used for authentication.

questions.explanationHtml: IPsec services allow for authentication, integrity, access control, and confidentiality. With IPsec, the information exchanged between remote sites can be encrypted and verified. Both remote-access and site-to-site VPNs can be deployed using IPsec.

questions.explanationHtml: IPsec can secure a path between two network devices. IPsec can provide the following security functions: Confidentiality – IPsec ensures confidentiality by using encryption. Integrity – IPsec ensures that data arrives unchanged at the destination using a hash algorithm, such as MD5 or SHA. Authentication – IPsec uses Internet Key Exchange (IKE) to authenticate users and devices that can carry out communication independently. IKE uses several types of authentication, including username and password, one-time password, biometrics, pre-shared keys (PSKs), and digital certificates. Secure key exchange- IPsec uses the Diffie-Hellman (DH) algorithm to provide a public key exchange method for two peers to establish a shared secret key.

Frame Relay would be a better choice than leased lines, but would be more expensive than implementing site-to-site VPNs. The other options refer to remote access VPNs which are better suited for connecting users to the corporate network versus interconnecting two or more networks.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of VPN allows multicast and broadcast traffic over a secure site-to-site VPN?
questions.explanationHtml: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) is a tunneling protocol that supports both multicast and broadcast traffic, which is essential for the operation of routing protocols over a VPN. Because standard IPsec tunnels are limited to unicast traffic, GRE over IPsec is used to encapsulate these non-unicast frames into GRE packets, which are then securely encrypted by IPsec for transport across the public network.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of VPN connects using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) feature?
questions.explanationHtml: When a client negotiates an SSL VPN connection with the VPN gateway, it connects using Transport Layer Security (TLS). TLS is the newer version of SSL and is sometimes expressed as SSL/TLS. The two terms are often used interchangeably.

questions.questionHtml: Which three types of VPNs are examples of enterprise-managed site-to-site VPNs? (Choose three.)
questions.explanationHtml: Enterprise-managed VPNs are created and managed by the organization using their own infrastructure to secure traffic across the internet. Within this category, IPsec VPNs, GRE over IPsec, and Cisco Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) are specifically classified as site-to-site solutions used to connect remote branch offices to a main site. Conversely, Layer 3 MPLS is a service provider-managed solution, while clientless SSL and client-based IPsec are types of remote access VPNs intended for individual mobile users.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of VPN uses a hub-and-spoke configuration to establish a full mesh topology?
questions.explanationHtml: Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) is a Cisco software solution designed to build multiple VPN tunnels in a dynamic and scalable manner. It specifically uses a hub-and-spoke configuration to establish what effectively becomes a full mesh topology; while spokes initially establish tunnels with a central hub, they can also obtain information from that hub to establish direct secure tunnels with each other as needed.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of VPN is the preferred choice for support and ease of deployment for remote access?
questions.explanationHtml: An SSL VPN is the preferred choice when support and ease of deployment are the primary considerations for remote access. While IPsec provides stronger security, SSL VPNs offer low connection complexity because they typically only require a web browser to establish a connection, making them easier to deploy across a wide range of devices without requiring specialized client software.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of VPN provides a flexible option to connect a central site with branch sites?
questions.explanationHtml: Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) is a Cisco software solution that simplifies tunnel configuration and provides a flexible option to connect a central site with branch sites. It uses a hub-and-spoke configuration to establish what effectively becomes a full mesh topology, allowing branch (spoke) sites to communicate through a central (hub) site and dynamically establish direct tunnels with each other.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of VPN involves the forwarding of traffic over the backbone through the use of labels distributed among core routers?
questions.explanationHtml: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) is used by service providers in their core networks to forward traffic through the MPLS backbone. This process involves the use of labels that are previously distributed among the core routers to determine the next hop for a packet. This mechanism allows the provider to create secure, virtual paths between client sites that effectively segregate their traffic from other customers.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of VPN involves a nonsecure tunneling protocol being encapsulated by IPsec?
questions.explanationHtml: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) is a non-secure tunneling protocol that can encapsulate various network layer protocols but lacks built-in encryption services. To secure the communication, a GRE packet is encapsulated into an IPsec packet, which provides the necessary encryption and authentication to protect the data as it travels across an untrusted network. This approach allows for the secure transport of multicast and routing protocol traffic, which standard IPsec VPNs cannot handle alone.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of VPN routes packets through virtual tunnel interfaces for encryption and forwarding?
questions.explanationHtml: IPsec Virtual Tunnel Interface (VTI) simplifies VPN configuration by applying IPsec settings to a virtual interface rather than mapping them statically to a physical interface. In this mechanism, packets are routed directly to the VTI, which then encrypts and forwards the traffic to the physical exit interface. Because the VTI is seen as a routable interface, it natively supports both unicast and multicast encrypted traffic, including routing protocols, without the need for additional GRE encapsulation.

title: QoS Concepts
summary: Covers the distinct bandwidth, delay, jitter, and loss characteristics of voice, video, and data traffic, and the QoS mechanisms used to manage them: classification and marking (CoS/DSCP), queuing, shaping vs. policing, congestion avoidance, and the trust boundary.

commands.description: Displays the QoS policy applied to an interface along with class-map match statistics, used to verify classification, marking, and queuing behavior.

terms.description: A set of techniques (classification/marking, queuing, shaping, policing) used to manage bandwidth, delay, jitter, and packet loss so time-sensitive traffic like voice and video receives preferential treatment over less-sensitive data traffic.
A 3-bit Layer 2 QoS marking field in the 802.1Q Ethernet frame header, providing 8 priority levels (0-7) that QoS-enabled switches can use to give preferential treatment to traffic.
A congestion-avoidance QoS mechanism that buffers excess packets in a queue and releases them over time, producing a smoothed output rate rather than dropping traffic.
A QoS mechanism that drops (or re-marks) traffic exceeding a configured maximum rate immediately, producing a saw-tooth output pattern rather than buffering it.

The point in the network, ideally as close to the traffic source as possible (e.g., the IP phone itself), where a device's traffic markings are accepted as trustworthy by the rest of the QoS-enabled network.
The process of analyzing traffic flows and determining which QoS class they belong to; classification must occur before a packet can be marked with a priority value.
The variation in the delay of received packets; along with delay/latency, jitter must be minimized by QoS for real-time voice and video traffic.
The simplest queuing mechanism; buffers and forwards packets strictly in arrival order with no prioritization or traffic-class awareness.

Smooth, predictable traffic (~200-byte packets every 20 ms); tolerates up to 150 ms latency, 30 ms jitter, 1% packet loss, and needs a minimum of ~30 Kbps bandwidth — low bandwidth need but very loss/delay sensitive.
Bursty, unpredictable traffic with packet size/volume varying every ~33 ms; requires latency no more than 400 ms, at least 384 Kbps bandwidth, and is less resilient to packet loss than voice.

Priority depends on whether the application is interactive/mission-critical (needs 1-2 second response time, higher priority) versus non-interactive (gets only leftover bandwidth); generally insensitive to delay/jitter but intolerant of loss.

Adding a value to a packet header (CoS at Layer 2, DSCP at Layer 3) so downstream devices can classify the packet and apply the correct QoS policy; should be done as close to the traffic source as possible, at the trust boundary.
A 6-bit Layer 3 QoS marking field in the IP header's ToS byte, providing up to 64 possible values/classes for finer-grained QoS treatment than the Layer 2 CoS field.

Mechanisms (e.g., FIFO, PQ, WFQ, CBWFQ, LLQ) that buffer and schedule packets for transmission based on priority when an interface is congested, ensuring higher-priority traffic classes are serviced first.

The three QoS models: best-effort (no special treatment, simplest and most scalable), IntServ (Integrated Services — per-flow bandwidth reservation via RSVP, does not scale), and DiffServ (Differentiated Services — traffic marked into classes/PHBs at the edge, the most widely deployed, scalable model).
The forwarding treatment (e.g., queuing/dropping priority) a router applies to a packet based solely on its DSCP marking, without needing per-flow state.

facts: QoS techniques (classification/marking, queuing, shaping, policing) manage bandwidth, delay, jitter, and packet loss so time-sensitive traffic like voice and video gets preferential treatment over ordinary data.
A packet must be classified into a traffic class before it can be marked with a priority value; marking should happen as close to the traffic source as possible.
CoS is a 3-bit Layer 2 field in the 802.1Q Ethernet header (8 priority levels, 0-7); DSCP is a 6-bit Layer 3 field in the IP header providing up to 64 distinct marking values.
The trust boundary is the point in the network, ideally as close to the source as possible (e.g., the IP phone itself), where a device's traffic markings are accepted as trustworthy.

Traffic shaping buffers and releases excess packets at a smoothed rate (delaying rather than dropping); traffic policing drops or re-marks traffic exceeding a configured rate, producing a sawtooth output pattern.
Voice traffic is smooth and predictable (~200-byte packets every 20ms), needs only ~30 Kbps, but tolerates at most 150ms latency, 30ms jitter, and 1% packet loss.
Video traffic is bursty and unpredictable, needs at least 384 Kbps, tolerates up to 400ms latency, and is actually less tolerant of packet loss than voice traffic.

Interactive/mission-critical data traffic should be prioritized for a 1-2 second response time; non-interactive data traffic gets only leftover bandwidth after voice, video, and critical data are served.
Common QoS queuing models include FIFO (no prioritization), CBWFQ (class-based fair queuing), and LLQ (low-latency queuing, which gives voice traffic strict-priority treatment).

WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection) is a congestion-avoidance technique that selectively drops lower-priority packets before a queue fills completely, helping to prevent TCP global synchronization.

Of the three QoS models, best-effort applies no special treatment and scales best, IntServ reserves guaranteed end-to-end bandwidth per flow via RSVP but does not scale to large networks, and DiffServ marks packets into classes at the network edge for scalable, though not per-flow-guaranteed, differentiated treatment — DiffServ is the model most widely deployed in production networks.

questions.explanationHtml: Video traffic is characterized as unpredictable, inconsistent, and bursty because the number and size of packets vary depending on the content being transmitted (e.g., action sequences require more data than static scenes). To maintain an acceptable user experience and prevent degradation like blurriness or unsynchronized audio, the network must ensure that latency does not exceed 400 ms. Conversely, video is less resilient to loss than voice and requires significantly higher bandwidth (at least 384 Kbps).

questions.questionHtml: Which type of QoS marking is applied to Ethernet frames?
questions.explanationHtml:
Topic 9.5.5
The class of service (CoS) marking allows a Layer 2 Ethernet frame to be marked with eight levels of priority (values 0–7). This marking can be used by QoS-enabled network devices to provide preferential traffic treatment.

questions.questionHtml: Refer to the exhibit. A network administrator has deployed QoS and has configured the network to mark traffic on the VoIP phones as well as the Layer 2 and Layer 3 switches. Where should initial marking occur to establish the trust boundary?
questions.explanationHtml: Traffic should be classified and marked as close to its source as possible. The trust boundary identifies at which device marked traffic should be trusted. Traffic marked on VoIP phones would be considered trusted as it moves into the enterprise network.

questions.questionHtml: What QoS step must occur before packets can be marked?
questions.explanationHtml: Before a packet can be marked, it must first be classified. Classification is the process of analyzing network traffic flows to determine which specific class they belong to based on defined criteria. Once the traffic class is determined through classification, the packet can then be marked with a priority value in its header (such as DSCP or CoS) so that other QoS tools can identify and treat the traffic according to the established policy.

questions.questionHtml: Refer to the exhibit. As traffic is forwarded out an egress interface with QoS treatment, which congestion avoidance technique is used?
questions.explanationHtml: Traffic shaping buffers excess packets in a queue and then forwards the traffic over increments of time, which creates a smoothed packet output rate. Traffic policing drops traffic when the amount of traffic reaches a configured maximum rate, which creates an output rate that appears as a saw-tooth with crests and troughs.

questions.questionHtml: Why is QoS an important issue in a converged network that combines voice, video, and data communications?

options.html: Data communications must be given the first priority.
options.text: Data communications must be given the first priority.

options.html: Voice and video communications are more sensitive to latency.
options.text: Voice and video communications are more sensitive to latency.

options.html: Legacy equipment is unable to transmit voice and video without QoS.
options.text: Legacy equipment is unable to transmit voice and video without QoS.

options.html: Data communications are sensitive to jitter.
options.text: Data communications are sensitive to jitter.

questions.explanationHtml: Without any QoS mechanisms in place, time-sensitive packets, such as voice and video, will be dropped with the same frequency as email and web browsing traffic.

questions.questionHtml: When QoS is implemented in a converged network, which two factors can be controlled to improve network performance for real-time traffic? (Choose two.)
questions.explanationHtml: Delay is the latency between a sending and receiving device. Jitter is the variation in the delay of the received packets. Both delay and jitter need to be controlled in order to support real-time voice and video traffic.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as having a high volume of data per packet?
questions.explanationHtml: Compared to voice traffic, video is described as having a higher volume of data per packet. While voice packets are typically small and predictable (approximately 200 bytes), video packets are significantly larger and vary in size based on the complexity and motion of the content being transmitted.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as not resilient to loss?
questions.explanationHtml: Video traffic tends to be unpredictable, inconsistent, and bursty compared to voice traffic. Compared to voice, video is less resilient to loss and has a higher volume of data per packet.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as predictable and smooth?
questions.explanationHtml: Voice traffic is specifically described as being predictable and smooth. It has known packet arrival times and a consistent bandwidth requirement, with packets typically arriving every 20 ms at a predictable size of 200 bytes. In contrast, video traffic is described as unpredictable and bursty, while general data traffic often has unpredictable bandwidth needs.

questions.questionHtml: Which queuing mechanism has no provision for prioritizing or buffering but simply forwards packets in the order they arrive?
questions.explanationHtml: FIFO (First-In, First-Out), also known as first-come, first-served, is the simplest queuing mechanism that buffers and forwards packets in the exact order they arrive. It has no concept of priority or traffic classes, meaning it makes no decisions to reorder packets based on importance; instead, it treats all packets equally within a single queue.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as requiring latency to be no more than 400 milliseconds (ms)?
questions.explanationHtml: Video traffic is described as requiring a one-way latency (delay) of no more than 400 milliseconds (ms) to maintain an acceptable user experience. In contrast, voice traffic is much more sensitive to delay and requires latency to be no more than 150 ms. General data traffic is typically classified as being relatively insensitive to both drops and delays.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as tending to be unpredictable, inconsistent, and bursty?
questions.explanationHtml: Video traffic is specifically described as tending to be unpredictable, inconsistent, and bursty. This is because the number and size of video packets vary significantly every 33 ms based on the complexity of the content; for example, rapidly changing action sequences require larger packets and higher volume compared to more static scenes. In contrast, voice traffic is defined as predictable and smooth.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as consisting of traffic that requires a higher priority if interactive?
questions.explanationHtml: While voice and video traffic are inherently sensitive to delay and always require high priority, data traffic priority is determined by specific factors. According to the sources, a network administrator must evaluate if data comes from an interactive application; if it is interactive and mission-critical, it should be prioritized to achieve a response time of 1 to 2 seconds. Non-interactive data, by contrast, is less sensitive to delay and can use leftover bandwidth.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as using either TCP or UDP depending on the need for error recovery?
questions.explanationHtml: Data traffic consists of applications that use either TCP or UDP based on their specific requirements. While real-time traffic like voice and video typically use UDP, data applications that have no tolerance for data loss (such as email and web pages) use TCP because it performs error recovery to ensure that any packets lost in transit are resent.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as consisting of traffic that gets a lower priority if it is not mission-critical?
questions.explanationHtml: The priority of data traffic is determined by whether the application is interactive or mission-critical. While voice and video traffic inherently require high priority, data traffic that is not mission-critical and not interactive is assigned a lower priority, essentially receiving only the leftover bandwidth after all other needs are met. In contrast, voice and video are always sensitive to delay and typically receive higher priority.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as being able to tolerate a certain amount of latency, jitter, and loss without any noticeable effects?
questions.explanationHtml: Voice traffic is described as smooth and predictable but very sensitive to delays. It can tolerate a specific amount of latency (up to 150 ms), jitter (up to 30 ms), and packet loss (up to 1%) without users experiencing any noticeable effects on quality. While video traffic has similar tolerances, it is considered less resilient to loss than voice. In contrast, data traffic is typically insensitive to delay and jitter but cannot tolerate any loss.

questions.questionHtml: What term describes adding a value to the packet header, as close to the source as possible, so that the packet matches a defined policy?
questions.explanationHtml: Traffic marking is the process of adding a specific value to the packet header (such as CoS at Layer 2 or DSCP at Layer 3). This allows subsequent network devices to identify the traffic class and apply defined forwarding policies accordingly. For maximum efficiency, marking should be performed as close to the source as possible to establish a trust boundary.

questions.questionHtml: What type of traffic is described as requiring at least 384 Kbps of bandwidth?
questions.explanationHtml: Video traffic is more demanding than voice traffic because of its higher volume of data per packet. It is specifically described as requiring at least 384 Kbps of bandwidth to maintain an acceptable user experience. In contrast, voice traffic requires a minimum of only 30 Kbps.

questions.questionHtml: Which QoS technique smooths packet output rate?
questions.explanationHtml: Traffic shaping is a QoS mechanism that retains excess packets in a queue and schedules them for transmission over time. This process results in a smoothed packet output rate. Unlike policing, which drops excess traffic immediately, shaping requires a queue and sufficient memory to buffer and delay packets for later transmission.

Configures the device to send syslog messages to the specified centralized syslog server.

Enables the device's SNMP agent to send unsolicited trap notifications to the configured manager immediately when a significant event occurs.

Globally enables LLDP on the device; unlike CDP, LLDP is disabled by default on most Cisco IOS platforms.
Enables an interface to send LLDP advertisements to its directly connected neighbor. Because LLDP is vendor-neutral (unlike CDP), transmit and receive must each be enabled separately.
Enables an interface to accept and process LLDP advertisements from its directly connected neighbor.
Displays detailed interface status and statistics, including whether the port is running full- or half-duplex; used to diagnose a duplex mismatch after a %CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH log message.
Displays a summary of directly connected Cisco devices discovered via CDP (device ID, local interface, holdtime, capability, platform, remote port).
Displays detailed CDP neighbor information, including the neighbor's IP address, IOS version, and platform — more detail than the summary 'show cdp neighbors'.
Displays a quick summary of each interface's IP address and up/down (line protocol) status; a common first troubleshooting command, though it does not show duplex settings.
Displays the IOS image filename and its source location (e.g., flash:), the configuration register value, uptime, and hardware details — used to confirm from where the router loaded its IOS image.
Reboots the router/switch; commonly used after a configuration register change or to complete password recovery.
Deletes the saved startup configuration in NVRAM, returning the device to factory defaults after the next reload.
Specifies which IOS image file the router should load at startup, overriding the default boot sequence.
Lists IOS image files and available space in flash memory, used to verify boot image availability.

terms.description: A Cisco-proprietary Layer 2 protocol that sends periodic advertisements to directly connected Cisco devices, sharing information such as device hostname, platform, IOS version, and interface types/numbers; can log %CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH when it detects conflicting duplex settings.

A vendor-neutral (IEEE 802.1AB) Layer 2 discovery protocol performing a function similar to CDP but working between devices from different vendors; transmit and receive must each be separately enabled.
A standard for logging system event messages; a syslog server acts as a centralized location keeping a historical record of messages sent from monitored network devices.

A protocol that synchronizes device clocks with a private master clock or public internet time server using a hierarchical stratum system (smaller stratum = closer to the Stratum 0 reference), ensuring consistent timestamps for correlating log and security events.

An application-layer protocol built on three elements: the SNMP manager (management software), SNMP agents (software modules on managed devices), and the MIB (information database); the manager polls agents via 'get' requests and receives unsolicited trap notifications.

Unsolicited messages sent by an SNMP agent to the manager immediately when a significant event occurs, eliminating the need for constant periodic polling and reducing load on network and agent resources.

The highest SNMPv3 security level, combining authentication (User-based Security Model with HMAC-MD5/SHA) with privacy (encryption via DES, 3DES, or AES); other levels are noAuth (community/username only) and auth (authentication only, no encryption).
The information database on a managed device that SNMP agents use to store operational data/statistics, queried by the SNMP manager.

A 16-bit software value (default 0x2102) that controls router boot behavior, such as where to load the IOS from and whether to load the startup-config; changed to 0x2142 during password recovery so the router ignores the startup-config on boot.
A bootstrap-level operating mode on Cisco devices used for low-level tasks such as password recovery and IOS image recovery when the full IOS cannot load normally.

Standard levels from 0 (Emergency, most severe) through 7 (Debugging, least severe: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging); 'logging trap {level}' sets the minimum severity forwarded to the syslog server.

Requires changing the configuration register (typically to 0x2142) in ROMMON so the router ignores the startup-config on boot, reloading, copying startup-config to running-config, setting a new password, saving, and resetting the register back to 0x2102 (config-register 0x2102) for the recovery to be permanent.
A simple, connectionless file transfer protocol commonly used to back up/restore IOS images and configuration files to/from a network server.
The SNMP manager (NMS) polls and receives data from SNMP agents running on managed devices; agents maintain a local MIB and respond to Get requests or send unsolicited Trap messages.

facts: CDP is Cisco-proprietary and works only between directly connected Cisco devices; LLDP is the vendor-neutral (IEEE 802.1AB) equivalent that works across multi-vendor gear, and unlike CDP, LLDP transmit and receive must be enabled separately per interface.

NTP synchronizes device clocks using a stratum hierarchy where lower numbers are closer to the authoritative reference clock (Stratum 0); show ntp associations detail reveals which device is the NTP master vs. client.
Syslog severity levels run from 0 (Emergency, most severe) to 7 (Debugging, least severe): 0-Emergency, 1-Alert, 2-Critical, 3-Error, 4-Warning, 5-Notice, 6-Informational, 7-Debugging.

SNMPv1/v2c authenticate only with a plain-text community string with no encryption; SNMPv3 adds three configurable security levels — noAuth (username/community match only), auth (HMAC MD5/SHA authentication, no encryption), and priv (authentication plus DES/3DES/AES encryption).
SNMP traps are unsolicited messages an agent sends to the manager the instant a significant event occurs, avoiding the overhead of constant polling.

The default IOS configuration register is 0x2102 (load IOS from flash, load startup-config from NVRAM); password recovery temporarily changes it to 0x2142 in ROMMON so the router skips the startup-config and existing passwords are bypassed.

Password recovery steps: set the register to 0x2142 in ROMMON, reload, copy startup-config to running-config to restore settings, set a new password, save the config, then reset the register back to 0x2102.

A %CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH log message flags a duplex conflict between neighbors; show interfaces reveals the actual duplex setting, while show cdp neighbors and show ip interface brief do not.

A duplex mismatch occurs when both connected devices are manually set to different duplex modes, or one autonegotiates while its peer is manually fixed at full-duplex (causing the autonegotiating side to fall back to half-duplex); a pure speed mismatch alone does not cause it.

SNMP operates with a manager (NMS) that polls agents using Get/Set messages and agents that respond and can also proactively send unsolicited Trap messages to the manager when a significant event occurs, avoiding constant polling overhead.

questions.questionHtml: Which two things should a network administrator modify on a router to perform password recovery? (Choose two.)
questions.explanationHtml: To perform password recovery, the administrator must first change the configuration register value (typically to 0x2142) while in ROMMON mode. This setting instructs the router to ignore the startup configuration file during the boot process, allowing access to the device without a password. Once the router has loaded, the administrator copies the original configuration into RAM, sets a new password, and then modifies the startup configuration file by saving the new settings to ensure the recovery is permanent.

questions.questionHtml: Which type of server would be used to keep a historical record of messages from monitored network devices?

questions.questionHtml: What protocol sends periodic advertisements between connected Cisco devices in order to learn device name, IOS version, and the number and type of interfaces?
questions.explanationHtml: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) is a Cisco proprietary Layer 2 protocol that runs on all Cisco devices. It sends periodic advertisements to physically connected Cisco neighbors to share critical information, including the device name (hostname), the hardware platform, the IOS version, and the number and type of interfaces. While LLDP performs similar functions, it is a vendor-neutral protocol, whereas CDP is specifically designed for connected Cisco equipment.

questions.questionHtml: What protocol synchronizes with a private master clock or with a publicly available server on the internet?
questions.explanationHtml: Network Time Protocol (NTP) allows network devices to synchronize their software clocks with an NTP server to ensure accurate and consistent timestamping across the infrastructure. When implemented, the protocol can be configured to synchronize with a private master clock or with a publicly available NTP server on the internet. Consistent time settings are critical for correlating events in system logs and for effective network troubleshooting.

questions.questionHtml: What protocol is a vendor-neutral Layer 2 protocol that advertises the identity and capabilities of the host device to other connected network devices?
questions.explanationHtml: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) is a vendor-neutral Layer 2 neighbor discovery protocol similar to CDP. It is designed to work with network devices from different manufacturers, allowing them to advertise their identity and capabilities (such as device name, type, and management address) to other physically connected Layer 2 devices. This makes LLDP an essential tool for mapping network topologies in multi-vendor environments.

questions.questionHtml: What protocol is used in a system that consists of three elements--a manager, agents, and an information database?
questions.explanationHtml: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is an application layer protocol that enables network administrators to monitor and manage network performance. An SNMP system is architecturally defined by three key elements: the SNMP manager (which runs management software), SNMP agents (software modules residing on managed devices), and the Management Information Base (MIB), which serves as the information database for storing device data and operational statistics.

questions.questionHtml: What protocol uses smaller stratum numbers to indicate that the server is closer to the authorized time source than larger stratum numbers?
questions.explanationHtml: The Network Time Protocol (NTP) utilizes a hierarchical system of time sources where each level is known as a stratum. Smaller stratum numbers indicate that a server is closer to the authoritative time source (Stratum 0 high-precision devices) compared to larger stratum numbers. For example, Stratum 1 devices are directly connected to the primary time source, while Stratum 2 devices synchronize their time using packets from Stratum 1 servers.

questions.questionHtml: What protocol allows the manager to poll agents to access information from the agent MIB?
questions.explanationHtml: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is an application layer protocol that facilitates communication between network managers and agents. The SNMP manager uses the agent to poll and query the MIB (Management Information Base) for device data and operational statistics using “get” requests.

questions.questionHtml: What protocol is a vendor-neutral Layer 2 discovery protocol that must be configured separately to transmit and receive information packets?
questions.explanationHtml: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) is a vendor-neutral Layer 2 discovery protocol. Unlike Cisco proprietary protocols, LLDP requires separate configuration for an interface to transmit and receive information packets using specific commands like lldp transmit and lldp receive.

questions.questionHtml: A technician is working on a Layer 2 switch and notices that a %CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH message keeps appearing for port G0/5. What command should the technician issue on the switch to start the troubleshooting process?
questions.explanationHtml: The %CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH message indicates that the local interface and its connected neighbor have conflicting duplex settings. To start troubleshooting, the technician must verify the operational status and configuration of the specific port mentioned in the error. The show interface g0/5 command provides detailed information, including whether the port is currently operating in full-duplex or half-duplex mode, allowing the technician to identify the mismatch.

Additionally, the authPriv level adds confidentiality by encrypting the data using algorithms like DES, 3DES, or AES.

questions.questionHtml: What protocol uses agents, that reside on managed devices, to collect and store information about the device and its operation?
questions.explanationHtml: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) uses agents — software running on each managed device — to collect and store information about the device and its operation in the MIB (Management Information Base). The SNMP manager (usually an NMS) polls agents to retrieve that information, and agents can also send unsolicited traps to the manager the moment a significant event occurs. Syslog centralizes log messages but has no agent/MIB architecture, TFTP simply transfers files, and CBWFQ is a QoS queuing mechanism.

title: Network Design
summary: Covers hierarchical three-tier and collapsed two-tier network design, the distinct roles of the access, distribution, and core layers, redundancy and failure-domain minimization, converged networks, and device-selection and documentation considerations.

terms.description: The portion of a network impacted when a critical device or link fails; good hierarchical design (e.g., redundant router/switch pairs in a switch block) limits its size, rather than simply buying larger-capacity equipment.
A single network infrastructure that carries voice, video, and data traffic together, reducing the cost and complexity of installing and managing separate networks for each traffic type.

A network design where the core and distribution layers are merged into a single device/layer; simpler and cheaper than a full three-tier hierarchy, but increases the size of the resulting failure domain.
A fixed-configuration access-layer switch family; supports only one active SVI on IOS versions prior to 15.x, and newer 2960-C models support PoE pass-through.
Provides network access to end-user devices and can supply Power over Ethernet (PoE); represents the network edge.
Aggregates access-layer connections, provides data traffic security/policy (e.g., ACLs), establishes Layer 3 routing boundaries, and connects to other/remote networks.
The high-speed network backbone; provides fast, redundant connectivity and aggregates all distribution-layer/campus blocks.

The recommended hierarchical design separating access, distribution, and core into distinct layers/devices for scalability and fault isolation, versus the simpler two-tier 'collapsed core' design that merges core and distribution.

A protocol family (HSRP, VRRP, GLBP) that provides default-gateway redundancy by letting two or more routers share a virtual IP/MAC address, so an access-layer failure of the active gateway does not disrupt end-host connectivity.
Cisco-proprietary FHRP where one router is active and forwards traffic for the virtual gateway IP while a standby router takes over on failure.

terms.full: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol / Gateway Load Balancing Protocol
terms.description: VRRP is the open-standard equivalent of HSRP; GLBP additionally load-balances outbound traffic across multiple gateway routers simultaneously rather than using a single active router.
Bundles multiple physical switch links into one logical link, increasing available bandwidth and providing redundancy without Spanning Tree blocking the extra links.

facts: In the three-tier hierarchical model, the access layer connects end-user devices and can supply PoE; the distribution layer aggregates access connections, enforces policy/security (e.g., ACLs), and forms Layer 3 routing boundaries; the core layer is the high-speed backbone that aggregates all distribution blocks.

A collapsed core (two-tier) design merges the core and distribution layers into one device/layer — simpler and cheaper, but it increases the size of the resulting failure domain versus a full three-tier design.

A failure domain is the portion of the network impacted when a critical device or link fails; good hierarchical/redundant design limits failure domain size rather than simply over-provisioning equipment.
A converged network carries voice, video, and data over a single infrastructure, reducing the cost and complexity of running separate parallel networks.
Redundancy — duplicate links, devices, and power supplies with no single point of failure — is a core hierarchical design principle that improves availability.

A logical topology diagram documents interface identifiers, connection types (LAN/WAN/point-to-point), and addressing; a physical topology diagram documents device type, OS/IOS version, and cable type/specification.
Device selection factors for hierarchical design include cost, port density, port speed/type, forwarding rates, and features like PoE, redundancy, and Layer 3 support.

FHRPs (HSRP, VRRP, GLBP) let two or more routers on the same LAN segment share a virtual IP and MAC address as the default gateway, so a physical router/link failure does not force every end host to be manually reconfigured; HSRP is Cisco-proprietary, VRRP is the open-standard equivalent, and GLBP additionally load-balances traffic across the participating routers.

EtherChannel bundles multiple physical switch links into a single logical link, providing both increased aggregate bandwidth and link redundancy while Spanning Tree treats the bundle as one port, avoiding blocked redundant links.

Topic 11.2.3
In order to best limit the of a failure domain, routers or multilayer switches can be deployed in pairs. The failure of a single device should not cause the network to go down. Installing redundant power supplies may protect a single device from a power failure, but if that device suffers from another type of problem, a redundant device would have been a better solution. Purchasing enterprise equipment that handles large flows of traffic will not provide extra reliability in times of an outage. If a collapsed core design is used, the core and distribution are collapsed into a single device, increasing the chance of a devastating outage.

title: Network Troubleshooting
summary: Covers structured troubleshooting methodologies (top-down, bottom-up, divide-and-conquer, educated guess), the symptom-gathering and scope-narrowing process, network baselining, and common show/debug commands used to isolate and resolve network problems.

commands.description: Sends ICMP echo requests to test basic Layer 3 reachability to a destination; e.g., a successful ping to an IP but a failed ping to the matching hostname points to a DNS problem, not a network outage.
Traces and displays the Layer 3 hop-by-hop path packets take to reach a destination, useful for isolating exactly where along a path connectivity fails.
Displays the IP routing table showing all known routes and their source (connected, static, or a routing protocol), used to verify a destination network is reachable.
Displays detailed status, statistics, and error counters (e.g., input/output errors, collisions, duplex) for interfaces; a key command for diagnosing physical/data-link layer problems.

commands.command: debug {feature} (e.g. ip nat, ip ospf events)
commands.description: Enables real-time, continuous display of internal processing events for a specific feature; a powerful troubleshooting tool that should be disabled with 'undebug all' when finished due to its CPU impact.
Aggregates output from many diagnostic show commands into one block, typically gathered for TAC/vendor support cases.
Displays per-process CPU utilization, used to identify a process consuming excessive router/switch CPU during troubleshooting.

terms.description: A recorded snapshot of normal network or system performance, established so future measurements can be compared against it to detect abnormal conditions.

A structured troubleshooting method where the technician makes an informed guess about which OSI layer is most likely causing the problem and starts testing there, working up or down as needed based on results.

A less-structured troubleshooting approach relying on the technician's experience and intuition to quickly isolate a probable cause; best suited to seasoned administrators, since it can be unreliable for less-experienced staff.

A structured method that starts testing at the Application layer and works downward through the OSI model; useful when the problem is suspected to be with a specific application or when many users/apps are affected.

A structured method that starts testing at the Physical layer and works upward through the OSI model; a good starting point when the root cause is unknown, since physical-layer issues are common and easy to check first.

Occurs when two connected interfaces use different duplex settings — either both manually configured to different modes, or one autonegotiates while the other is manually fixed at full-duplex (the autonegotiating side then defaults to half-duplex) — causing interface errors and late collisions. A pure speed mismatch alone does not cause it.

Cisco's default, topology-driven Layer 3 switching mechanism that uses the FIB and adjacency table (built proactively from the routing table and ARP table) to forward packets without per-packet control-plane lookups.
A CEF lookup table of destination network prefixes and their next hops, pre-populated from the router's IP routing table to enable fast forwarding decisions.
A CEF table containing Layer 2 next-hop rewrite (MAC address) information for directly connected next hops, pre-populated from the router's ARP table.
Network documentation showing interface identifiers, connection types (LAN, WAN, point-to-point), and addressing/protocol information, as opposed to physical layout.
Network documentation showing device type, OS/IOS version, and cable type/specification/identifiers — the physical realities of the installation.

Resolves domain names to IP addresses; if a ping to an IP address succeeds but a ping to the corresponding domain name fails, this points to a DNS resolution problem rather than a network reachability problem.

terms.full: Protocol analyzer and Time Domain Reflectometer
terms.description: A protocol analyzer (e.g., Wireshark) captures and decodes network traffic for troubleshooting; a TDR/cable tester sends a signal down a cable to locate breaks, shorts, or length problems.

facts: Structured troubleshooting methods include top-down (starts at the application layer, works down), bottom-up (starts at the physical layer, works up), and divide-and-conquer (starts at a layer based on an informed guess, then moves up or down from the result).

The educated-guess ('shoot-from-the-hip') method relies on experience/intuition to jump straight to a likely cause; it suits seasoned admins but is risky for less-experienced staff, who should use structured methods instead.
A network baseline is a recorded snapshot of normal performance used as a reference to detect abnormal conditions in future measurements.
During symptom gathering, the 'narrow the scope' step determines whether the problem lies at the core, distribution, or access layer before pinpointing specific equipment.

In Cisco Express Forwarding (CEF), the FIB is pre-populated from the IP routing table and the adjacency table (Layer 2 rewrite info) is pre-populated from the ARP table, enabling hardware-speed forwarding without per-packet lookups.
If a ping to a server's IP address succeeds but a ping to its domain name fails, the problem is DNS name resolution, not network reachability.
show version reveals the IOS image location, IOS version, configuration register value, and uptime — useful for confirming where/how the device booted.
'show tech-support' aggregates output from numerous diagnostic show commands into a single block, commonly captured for escalation to Cisco TAC or vendor support during complex troubleshooting.

questions.questionHtml: A user reports that when the corporate web page URL is entered on a web browser, an error message indicates that the page cannot be displayed. The help-desk technician asks the user to enter the IP address of the web server to see if the page can be displayed. Which troubleshooting method is being used by the technician?
questions.explanationHtml: The technician is using the divide-and-conquer method by making an informed guess based on symptoms to select a specific layer to start the investigation. By asking the user to enter the IP address instead of the URL, the technician is attempting to determine if the issue is a name resolution (DNS) problem or a connectivity issue at a lower layer. If the web page displays using the IP address, the technician has successfully “divided” the problem and knows the layers below the Application layer are functioning correctly.

questions.questionHtml: In which step of gathering symptoms does the network engineer determine if the problem is at the core, distribution, or access layer of the network?

title: Network Virtualization
summary: Covers cloud computing service and deployment models, server virtualization and Type 1 vs. Type 2 hypervisors, live migration, and software-defined networking concepts including controllers, northbound/southbound APIs, and Cisco ACI/APIC.

facts: Type 1 ('bare metal') hypervisors install directly on server hardware with no host OS, need a separate management console, and are the standard for efficient enterprise/data-center server consolidation; Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors run atop an existing OS, need no management console, and suit consumer/experimental use.

Server virtualization abstracts the OS from the underlying hardware, letting multiple independent VM instances run in parallel on one physical server and consolidating otherwise-idle hardware resources.
Live migration moves a running VM to another (potentially distant) physical host with minimal downtime, supporting disaster recovery since the DR site doesn't need identical hardware.

The three cloud service models are IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service — virtualized compute/storage/network), PaaS (Platform as a Service — a development/deployment environment), and SaaS (Software as a Service — ready-to-use applications delivered over the internet).

Cloud deployment models include public cloud (services offered to the general public), private cloud (dedicated to a single organization), hybrid cloud (a mix of public and private), and community cloud (shared by organizations with common concerns).

SDN separates the control plane from the data plane, centralizing network intelligence in an SDN controller; northbound APIs let the controller talk to business applications, while southbound APIs let it program downstream switches/routers directly.

Cisco ACI uses a two-tier spine-leaf fabric (every leaf connects to every spine, leaves never connect directly to each other, keeping all endpoints one hop apart), centrally managed by the APIC controller.

NFV (Network Functions Virtualization) decouples network functions such as firewalls, routers, and load balancers from dedicated proprietary appliances so they run as software instances on standard servers/VMs; it is complementary to, but distinct from, SDN, which centralizes the control plane.

SDN separates network device functionality into three planes: the data plane (actual packet forwarding hardware), the control plane (routing/forwarding decision logic, centralized in an SDN controller), and the management plane (device configuration and monitoring).

questions.explanationHtml: A data center is a dedicated facility used for the storage and processing of data, which can be managed by an in-house IT department or leased from an offsite provider. questions.questionHtml: A company has consolidated a number of servers and it is looking for a program or firmware to create and control virtual machines which have access to all the hardware of the consolidated servers. What service or technology would support this requirement?
questions.explanationHtml: A Type-1 hypervisor, also known as a “bare metal” approach, is a program or firmware installed directly on the physical hardware of a server. This allows the hypervisor to create and control virtual machines (VMs) that have direct access to all hardware resources, such as CPUs, memory, and disk controllers. Because they lack the overhead of a host operating system, Type-1 hypervisors are highly efficient and are the standard choice for server consolidation in enterprise and data center environments.

title: Network Automation
summary: Covers data formats used in network automation (JSON, XML, YAML), REST/RESTful API architecture and HTTP methods, and configuration management tools (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, SaltStack) and their agent/agentless and push/pull models.

terms.description: A lightweight data format used for network automation; an object is one or more key/value pairs enclosed in curly braces { } with double-quoted string keys separated from values by a colon; an array is an ordered, comma-separated list of values enclosed in square brackets [ ].
A data format for network automation where data values are enclosed within matching start and end tags, e.g. <tag>data</tag>.

A human-readable data format for network automation that represents key/value pairs separated by a colon (no quotation marks) and uses indentation rather than brackets or commas to define structure; commonly used for configuration-management files (e.g., Ansible playbooks).

The most widely used web service API architecture (over 80% of web service APIs), using standard HTTP methods against addressable resources; a RESTful request's query portion typically specifies the format (JSON/XML/YAML), a key (for authentication), and parameters (request-specific data).

terms.full: HTTP request methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE)
terms.description: The standard verbs used by RESTful APIs to perform CRUD operations on a resource: GET retrieves data, POST creates a new resource, PUT replaces/updates a full resource, PATCH partially updates a resource, and DELETE removes a resource.
An API used only within an organization to give internal users/applications (e.g., employees on mobile devices) access to internal data and services; not exposed to outside parties.

URI is the umbrella term identifying a resource (including protocol, host, path, and fragment); URL specifies the protocol+location used to retrieve a resource; URN names a resource (host/path) without the protocol.

Automation tools used to configure and manage devices at scale. Ansible is agentless and push-based (uses SSH and YAML playbooks); Puppet and Chef are agent-based and pull-based (managed nodes periodically pull config from a central server); SaltStack can operate in both agent-based (push, using a 'minion') and agentless modes.

terms.full: Yet Another Next Generation (data modeling language)
terms.description: A data modeling language used to define the structure, syntax, and semantics of configuration and state data that NETCONF/RESTCONF operations manipulate on a device.
An IETF network management protocol that uses XML-encoded remote procedure calls over SSH to install, manipulate, and retrieve device configuration data defined by YANG models.
A protocol that provides a REST-like HTTP interface (using JSON or XML) to a device's YANG-modeled configuration and state data, combining NETCONF's data model with RESTful HTTP methods.
A defined set of rules that lets one software application request services or data from another (e.g., a network controller), forming the general concept underlying REST/RESTful APIs.

facts: JSON encloses objects (comma-separated key/value pairs with double-quoted keys) in curly braces {}, and ordered arrays in square brackets []; XML wraps data in matching <tag>...</tag> pairs; YAML uses unquoted key:value pairs and indentation instead of brackets/commas.

REST/RESTful APIs account for more than 80% of web service APIs and use standard HTTP methods against addressable resources; a request's query string typically specifies the data format (JSON/XML/YAML), an authentication key, and request parameters.
The core HTTP methods used by REST APIs map to CRUD operations: GET (read/retrieve), POST (create), PUT (replace/fully update), PATCH (partially update), and DELETE (remove).

Ansible is agentless and push-based (uses SSH, playbooks written in YAML); Puppet is agent-based and pull-based (Puppet Master/agent model, manifests written in Ruby); Chef is agent-based and pull-based (uses Ruby 'recipes' with a Chef Workstation/Server model); SaltStack can run agent-based ('minion') or agentless and is primarily push-based, using YAML.
Network programmability shifts configuration from manual, per-device CLI entry to centralized, script/API-driven automation applied consistently across many devices at once.

YANG is a data modeling language that defines the structure of configuration and operational state data on a network device; NETCONF (XML over SSH) and RESTCONF (JSON/XML over HTTP) are the protocols used to actually read and manipulate that YANG-modeled data.
